claim: The asexual freshwater planarian is a constitutive adult whose central nervous system (CNS) is in a state of constant homeostatic neurogenesis.
source: The asexual freshwater planarian is a constitutive adult, whose central nervous system (CNS) is in a state of constant homeostatic neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract describing the biological context of the study.

claim: Smed-nkx2.1 and Smed-arx are required for the maintenance of cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons in the planarian CNS.
source: We have identified two planarian homeobox transcription factors, Smed-nkx2.1 and Smed-arx, which are required for the maintenance of cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons in the planarian CNS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically RNAi knockdown experiments showing loss of these neuronal populations.

claim: Cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons produce the planarian hedgehog ligand (Smed-hh).
source: These very same neurons also produce the planarian hedgehog ligand (Smed-hh), which appears to communicate with brain-adjacent stem cells to promote normal levels of neurogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by double fluorescent in situ hybridization (dFISH) data showing co-expression of hh with markers of these neuronal subtypes.

claim: The planarian hedgehog ligand communicates with brain-adjacent stem cells to promote normal levels of neurogenesis.
source: These very same neurons also produce the planarian hedgehog ligand (Smed-hh), which appears to communicate with brain-adjacent stem cells to promote normal levels of neurogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing expression of hh transduction machinery in stem cells and reduced neurogenesis upon hh knockdown.

claim: Planarian stem cells nearby the brain express core hh signal transduction genes.
source: Planarian stem cells nearby the brain express core hh signal transduction genes, and consistent hh signaling levels are required to maintain normal production of neural progenitor cells and new mature cholinergic neurons, revealing an important mitogenic role for the planarian hh signaling molecule in the adult CNS.
evidence: This is supported by dFISH experiments and single-cell RNA sequencing data showing expression of ptc, smo, and gli-1 in piwi-1+ stem cells.

claim: Consistent hh signaling levels are required to maintain normal production of neural progenitor cells and new mature cholinergic neurons.
source: Planarian stem cells nearby the brain express core hh signal transduction genes, and consistent hh signaling levels are required to maintain normal production of neural progenitor cells and new mature cholinergic neurons, revealing an important mitogenic role for the planarian hh signaling molecule in the adult CNS.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing reduced neural progenitor markers and BrdU incorporation in newly generated neurons upon hh knockdown.

claim: The planarian hh signaling molecule has an important mitogenic role in the adult CNS.
source: Planarian stem cells nearby the brain express core hh signal transduction genes, and consistent hh signaling levels are required to maintain normal production of neural progenitor cells and new mature cholinergic neurons, revealing an important mitogenic role for the planarian hh signaling molecule in the adult CNS.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing effects on neural progenitor production and neurogenesis.

claim: Homeostatic adult neurogenesis is a common trait shared by many disparate organisms including rodents, birds, flies, and humans.
source: Once thought to be a non-existent phenomenon, homeostatic adult neurogenesis is a common trait shared by many disparate organisms including rodents, birds, flies, and humans (Altman, 1962, 1969; Doetsch et al., 1999; Goldman and Nottebohm, 1983; Eriksson et al., 1998; Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Levels of neuronal turnover are tightly limited in rodents, birds, flies, and humans.
source: However, levels of neuronal turnover are tightly limited in these animals (Obernier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The highest known site of adult homeostatic neurogenesis in the human central nervous system is the hippocampus, where annual neuronal turnover rates are estimated to be only 1.75%.
source: In fact, the highest known site of adult homeostatic neurogenesis in the human central nervous system (CNS) is the hippocampus, where annual neuronal turnover rates are estimated to be only 1.75% (Spalding et al., 2013; Sanai et al., 2011; Bergmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult neurogenesis in most animals depends on the action of ectodermally derived neural stem cells, which have radial-glial character and are integrated into a stable niche microenvironment.
source: Adult neurogenesis in most animals depends on the action of ectodermally derived neural stem cells, which have radial-glial character and are integrated into a stable niche microenvironment.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neural stem cells.

claim: Extrinsic signals such as wingless (Wnt), sonic hedgehog (Shh), and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) act to finely control neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: Extrinsic signals such as wingless (Wnt), sonic hedgehog (Shh), and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) act to finely control neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation (Silva-Vargas et al., 2013; Lehtinen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The asexual strain of the freshwater planarian, Schmidtea mediterranea, is a constitutive adult flatworm (Lophotrochozoan) that challenges the dogma of low rates of adult neurogenesis.
source: The asexual strain of the freshwater planarian, Schmidtea mediterranea (S. mediterranea), is a constitutive adult flatworm (Lophotrochozoan) that challenges the dogma of low rates of adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological characteristics of the study organism.

claim: S. mediterranea constantly turns over its brain.
source: Not only does S. mediterranea constantly turnover its brain, but also it is capable of complete brain regeneration within only two weeks following decapitation (Cebria, 2007; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: S. mediterranea is capable of complete brain regeneration within only two weeks following decapitation.
source: Not only does S. mediterranea constantly turnover its brain, but also it is capable of complete brain regeneration within only two weeks following decapitation (Cebria, 2007; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The uninjured planarian CNS is a highly dynamic organ, which can adjust its size through the addition or subtraction of mature neurons to maintain consistent proportions with the rest of the body as it grows and shrinks.
source: In addition, the uninjured planarian CNS is known to be a highly dynamic organ, which can adjust its size through the addition or subtraction of mature neurons to maintain consistent proportions with the rest of the body as it grows and shrinks, respectively (Baguñá and Romero, 1981 ; Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Planarian regenerative feats and high levels of homeostatic neurogenesis are accomplished in the absence of a recognizable neuroepithelium, and without any definitive neural stem cells.
source: Amazingly, these regenerative feats and high levels of homeostatic neurogenesis are accomplished in the absence of a recognizable neuroepithelium, and without any definitive neural stem cells (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Brain-derived Wnt signals have been shown to influence the neurogenic output of planarian stem cells (neoblasts) during regeneration.
source: Recently, brain-derived Wnt signals have been shown to influence the neurogenic output of planarian stem cells (neoblasts) during regeneration (Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: nkx2.1 and arx act to specify cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons within the ventral-medial (VM) region of the planarian CNS.
source: Here, we have identified two planarian homeodomain transcription factors, Smed-nkx2.1 and Smed-arx (henceforth referred to as nkx2.1 and arx), which act to specify cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons within the ventral-medial (VM) region of the planarian CNS.
evidence: This is supported by expression data and RNAi experiments showing loss of these neuronal populations.

claim: VM neural cell types are a major source of the planarian hedgehog ligand.
source: Interestingly, these very same VM neural cell types are a major source of the planarian hedgehog ligand (Smed-hh; henceforth referred to as hh) (Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by dFISH data in the manuscript and citations to prior research.

claim: A novel neoblast population exists which are nkx2.1+ or arx+, express the core machinery for the reception of hh and Wnt signals, and are located adjacent to hh+ VM neurons.
source: We also describe a novel neoblast population, which are nkx2.1+ or arx+, express the core machinery for the reception of hh and Wnt signals, and are located adjacent to hh+ VM neurons.
evidence: This is supported by dFISH experiments and single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Consistent hh signaling within the neoblast microenvironment is required to promote normal homeostatic neurogenesis of the VM neuronal population.
source: Finally, we present evidence that consistent hh signaling within this neoblast microenvironment is required to promote normal homeostatic neurogenesis of the VM neuronal population.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing reduced neurogenesis upon hh knockdown.

claim: A hh signaling axis positively modulates VM neurogenesis through distinct progenitor cells.
source: In total, we identify a hh signaling axis that positively modulates VM neurogenesis through distinct progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: All nkx2.1(RNAi) animals exhibited a unique behavioral defect characterized by tonic muscular contractions that bend the head dorsally, so that it is perpendicular with the rest of the body.
source: A unique behavioral defect was observed in all nkx2.1(RNAi) animals, characterized by tonic muscular contractions that bend the head dorsally, so that it is perpendicular with the rest of the body.
evidence: This is an observation from the RNAi experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Some nkx2.1(RNAi) worms end up on their lateral body edge, causing these animals to move in tight circles, compared to control(RNAi) animals which move in straight lines on their ventral surface.
source: Interestingly, some of these nkx2.1(RNAi) worms end up on their lateral body edge, causing these animals to move in tight circles, compared to control(RNAi) animals which move in straight lines on their ventral surface (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the RNAi experiments, with reference to video data.

claim: arx(RNAi) animals do not display overt behavioral defects, except when flipped onto their dorsal side where these worms have difficulty to corkscrew in order to reorient onto their ventral surface compared to control(RNAi) and wild-type animals.
source: In contrast, arx(RNAi) animals do not display overt behavioral defects, except when flipped onto their dorsal side where these worms have difficulty to corkscrew in order to reorient onto their ventral surface compared to control(RNAi) and wild-type animals (Videos 1 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the RNAi experiments, with reference to video data.

claim: nkx2.1 exhibited broad expression throughout the body but was clearly present within the CNS.
source: nkx2.1 exhibited broad expression throughout the body but was clearly present within the CNS (black arrow), whereas arx expression was spatially restricted to the medial CNS, including the anterior brain and the full length of the ventral nerve cords (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: arx expression was spatially restricted to the medial CNS, including the anterior brain and the full length of the ventral nerve cords.
source: nkx2.1 exhibited broad expression throughout the body but was clearly present within the CNS (black arrow), whereas arx expression was spatially restricted to the medial CNS, including the anterior brain and the full length of the ventral nerve cords (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Transverse sections through the anterior-posterior (A-P) midpoint of the brain highlighted the concentrated expression of arx within the ventral-medial region of each brain lobe.
source: Transverse sections through the anterior-posterior (A-P) midpoint of the brain enabled imaging in greater spatial detail and highlighted the concentrated expression of arx within the ventral-medial region of each brain lobe (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of nkx2.1 and arx was observed within a few isolated cells in between the brain lobes, a region largely populated by adult stem cells.
source: In addition, expression of nkx2.1 and arx was observed within a few isolated cells in between the brain lobes, a region largely populated by adult stem cells (Figure 1B, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is based on fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 36.89 ± 5.46% of VM cholinergic neurons expressed nkx2.1.
source: A considerable proportion of cholinergic neurons expressed nkx2.1 in both the VM (36.89 ± 5.46%) and DL (23.33 ± 5.13%) brain regions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 23.33 ± 5.13% of DL cholinergic neurons expressed nkx2.1.
source: A considerable proportion of cholinergic neurons expressed nkx2.1 in both the VM (36.89 ± 5.46%) and DL (23.33 ± 5.13%) brain regions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 63.21 ± 4.35% of VM cholinergic neurons expressed arx.
source: In contrast, arx expression was more heavily biased toward the VM brain region, where 63.21 ± 4.35% of cholinergic neurons expressed this transcription factor (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Planarian GABAergic neurons are present in two spatially distinct VM and DL subgroups.
source: Planarian GABAergic neurons (gad+) are present in two spatially distinct VM and DL subgroups (Figure 1D) (Nishimura et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to prior research.

claim: 98.82 ± 2.63% of VM GABAergic neurons expressed nkx2.1.
source: Within the VM GABAergic neuron population, virtually all cells that were imaged expressed nkx2.1 (98.82 ± 2.63%), whereas expression of arx was not detected (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: arx expression was not detected in VM GABAergic neurons.
source: Within the VM GABAergic neuron population, virtually all cells that were imaged expressed nkx2.1 (98.82 ± 2.63%), whereas expression of arx was not detected (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The DL subgroup of GABAergic neurons did not exhibit significant expression of either nkx2.1 or arx.
source: In contrast, the DL subgroup of GABAergic neurons did not exhibit significant expression of either transcription factor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 76.9 ± 6.66% of octopaminergic neurons exhibited nkx2.1 expression.
source: Interestingly, expression of both transcription factors was observed within this neural cell group, with 76.9 ± 6.66% of octopaminergic neurons exhibiting nkx2.1 expression, while a lower proportion were arx+ (33.44 ± 6.54%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 33.44 ± 6.54% of octopaminergic neurons were arx+.
source: Interestingly, expression of both transcription factors was observed within this neural cell group, with 76.9 ± 6.66% of octopaminergic neurons exhibiting nkx2.1 expression, while a lower proportion were arx+ (33.44 ± 6.54%) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: arx(RNAi) worms exhibited a near 40% reduction in the number of VM cholinergic neurons.
source: Strikingly, arx(RNAi) worms exhibited a near 40% reduction in the number of VM cholinergic neurons, whereas DL neurons were largely unchanged (Figure 2A,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: DL cholinergic neurons were largely unchanged in arx(RNAi) worms.
source: Strikingly, arx(RNAi) worms exhibited a near 40% reduction in the number of VM cholinergic neurons, whereas DL neurons were largely unchanged (Figure 2A,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: nxk2.1(RNAi) worms displayed no detectable changes in the average number of both VM and DL cholinergic neurons.
source: In contrast, nxk2.1(RNAi) worms displayed no detectable changes in the average number of both VM and DL cholinergic neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: arx is required for the maintenance of VM cholinergic neurons.
source: This very specific loss of VM cholinergic neurons in arx(RNAi) worms, combined with the evidence that arx was expressed by >60% of these neurons, demonstrated that arx was required for the maintenance of VM cholinergic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi and expression data.

claim: nkx2.1(RNAi) worms exhibited a complete loss of all VM GABAergic neurons, while leaving DL neurons intact.
source: In contrast, nkx2.1(RNAi) worms exhibited a complete loss of all VM GABAergic neurons, while leaving DL neurons intact (Figure 2B,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: nkx2.1 acts in the maintenance of VM GABAergic neurons.
source: Combined with the above dFISH data, the ablation of all VM GABAergic neurons demonstrated that nkx2.1 acts in the maintenance of this neural subtype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi and expression data.

claim: arx(RNAi) animals exhibited no loss of GABAergic neurons in either the VM or the DL subgroups.
source: As expected, arx(RNAi) animals exhibited no loss of GABAergic neurons in either the VM or the DL subgroups (Figure 2B,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both nkx2.1(RNAi) and arx(RNAi) animals exhibited a significant reduction in the number of octopaminergic neurons.
source: Interestingly, both nkx2.1(RNAi) and arx(RNAi) animals exhibited a significant reduction in the number of octopaminergic neurons, which correlated with the degree of expression for each transcription factor within this neural cell type (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: nkx2.1(RNAi) animals exhibited a > 60% reduction in octopaminergic neurons.
source: While nkx2.1(RNAi) animals exhibited a > 60% reduction in octopaminergic neurons, arx(RNAi) worms displayed a more modest but significant ~ 25% reduction (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: arx(RNAi) worms displayed a ~ 25% reduction in octopaminergic neurons.
source: While nkx2.1(RNAi) animals exhibited a > 60% reduction in octopaminergic neurons, arx(RNAi) worms displayed a more modest but significant ~ 25% reduction (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The neurons lost in nkx2.1(RNAi) or arx(RNAi) animals were located in the VM region of the planarian brain.
source: It should also be noted that the neurons lost in nkx2.1(RNAi) or arx(RNAi) animals were located in the VM region of the planarian brain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RNAi of nkx2.1 or arx had no appreciable effect on the dopaminergic and serotonergic neuron populations.
source: As expected, RNAi of nkx2.1 or arx had no appreciable effect on the dopaminergic and serotonergic neuron populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The maintenance roles of nkx2.1 and arx are limited to the VM cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neuronal cell populations.
source: Therefore, the maintenance roles of nkx2.1 and arx are limited to the VM cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neuronal cell populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi experiments showing specific effects on these neuronal populations.

claim: The planarian CNS is a major site of expression for the single hedgehog ligand in planarians.
source: Previous studies have shown that the planarian CNS is a major site of expression for the single hedgehog ligand in planarians (Smed-hh; henceforth referred to as hh) (Figure 3A) (Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior research.

claim: Transverse sections through the brain highlighted hh expression within the VM regions of each brain lobe, similar to that of arx.
source: However, it is unknown what specific cells express this signal and what cells respond to it. Transverse sections through the brain highlighted hh expression within the VM regions of each brain lobe, similar to that of arx (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 23.17 ± 2.88% of VM cholinergic neurons expressed hh.
source: As with arx, hh expression within cholinergic neurons was heavily biased toward the VM region of the brain lobe, where 23.17 ± 2.88% of these neurons expressed the signaling molecule (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 98.08 ± 3.85% of VM GABAergic neurons expressed hh.
source: In addition, hh was expressed by nearly all VM GABAergic neurons (98.08 ± 3.85), as well as a considerable proportion of octopaminergic neurons (33.7 ± 2.23%) (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: 33.7 ± 2.23% of octopaminergic neurons expressed hh.
source: In addition, hh was expressed by nearly all VM GABAergic neurons (98.08 ± 3.85), as well as a considerable proportion of octopaminergic neurons (33.7 ± 2.23%) (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: VM neurons appear to be the main source of the planarian hh signaling molecule.
source: Although a limited number of DL GABAergic, dopaminergic, and serotonergic neurons exhibited hh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), VM neurons appear to be the main source of the planarian hh signaling molecule.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dFISH data showing predominant expression in VM neurons.

claim: WISH experiments demonstrated a clear reduction in hh expression within the medial CNS of arx(RNAi) worms.
source: WISH experiments demonstrated a clear reduction in hh expression within the medial CNS of arx(RNAi) worms (Figure 3F; white arrows), while silencing nkx2.1 had little effect on hh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Silencing nkx2.1 had little effect on hh expression.
source: WISH experiments demonstrated a clear reduction in hh expression within the medial CNS of arx(RNAi) worms (Figure 3F; white arrows), while silencing nkx2.1 had little effect on hh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: arx(RNAi) animals exhibited a near 60% reduction in the number of VM hh+ neurons.
source: This analysis revealed a near 60% reduction in the number of VM hh+ neurons in arx(RNAi) animals (Figure 3F–G), but no significant loss of hh+ cells in the DL brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: There was no significant loss of hh+ cells in the DL brain in arx(RNAi) animals.
source: This analysis revealed a near 60% reduction in the number of VM hh+ neurons in arx(RNAi) animals (Figure 3F–G), but no significant loss of hh+ cells in the DL brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Silencing of nkx2.1 did not significantly alter hh expression levels in either brain region.
source: In contrast, silencing of nkx2.1 did not significantly alter hh expression levels in either brain region (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: hh expression in the VM domain of the planarian brain requires arx gene function.
source: While it is unclear whether arx directly regulates hh expression in VM neurons, or whether reduced hh expression is related to a loss of VM cholinergic neurons, it is clear that hh expression in the VM domain of the planarian brain requires arx gene function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi experiments showing reduced hh expression upon arx knockdown.

claim: hh expression was detected in 4/39 neurons, and a single stem cell, but no other cell types from the scRNAseq dataset.
source: From this group of sequenced cells, hh expression was detected in 4/39 neurons, and a single stem cell, but no other cell types (Figure 3H), supporting previous data that hh expression is largely restricted to the nervous system.
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: nkx2.1 was detected in two sequenced neurons.
source: In addition, these 39 sequenced neurons were examined for expression of nkx2.1 and arx, which were detected in two and six neurons, respectively, with two of these cells displaying co-expression with hh (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: arx was detected in six sequenced neurons.
source: In addition, these 39 sequenced neurons were examined for expression of nkx2.1 and arx, which were detected in two and six neurons, respectively, with two of these cells displaying co-expression with hh (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Two sequenced neurons displayed co-expression of nkx2.1 or arx with hh.
source: In addition, these 39 sequenced neurons were examined for expression of nkx2.1 and arx, which were detected in two and six neurons, respectively, with two of these cells displaying co-expression with hh (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Five of the nine sequenced neurons expressing nkx2.1 or arx were chat+ cholinergic neurons.
source: High expression levels of common mature neuron markers (Smed-synaptotagmin, Smed-synapsin, Smed-pc2) were found in all nine sequenced cells, and more specifically, five of these cells were chat+ cholinergic neurons (Figure 3I) (Agata et al., 1998; Cebrià, 2008).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Each of the nine neurons expressing nkx2.1 or arx expressed a unique combination of neuropeptides, transcription factors, RNA-binding proteins, and Wnts with known or putative roles in neuronal specification and patterning.
source: In addition, each of these nine neurons expressed a unique combination of neuropeptides (Collins et al., 2010), transcription factors (Cowles et al., 2013, 2014; Currie and Pearson, 2013; Pineda et al., 2002), RNA-binding proteins (Higuchi et al., 2008; Koushika et al., 1996), and even 2 Wnts with known or putative roles in neuronal specification and patterning (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3I, with citations to prior research.

claim: The planarian hh ligand is expressed by mature neurons.
source: This in silico data acts to further confirm that the planarian hh ligand is expressed by mature neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: hh signaling activity can influence global proliferation levels.
source: Considering that VM planarian neurons are a major source of the hh signaling molecule (Figure 3) (Rink et al., 2009; Yazawa et al., 2009), it was of great interest to discover what cells and tissues might be the target of this brain-derived signaling molecule. Previous observations have shown that hh signaling activity can influence global proliferation levels (Rink et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Many piwi-1+ ASCs in between the two brain lobes co-expressed the ptc receptor.
source: However, when piwi-1+ ASCs (Reddien et al., 2005b) were visualized in between the two brain lobes, many were observed to co-express the ptc receptor (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on dFISH experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: smo and gli-1 expression was detected in brain-adjacent ASCs.
source: Similarly, smo and gli-1 expression was detected in brain-adjacent ASCs (Figure 4B), providing support for the notion that planarian stem cells might be a target of brain-derived hh signals.
evidence: This is based on dFISH experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Approximately 30% (56/168 cells) of sequenced head stem cells expressed at least one of ptc, smo, or gli-1.
source: Approximately 30% (56/168 cells) expressed at least one of ptc, smo, or gli-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Approximately half of the sequenced head stem cells (81/168) expressed at least one of the nine planarian Frizzled (fz) receptors.
source: Interestingly, approximately half of these sequenced cells (81/168) also expressed at least one of the nine planarian Frizzled (fz) receptors (which bind Wnt ligands) (Gurley et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4C, with citations to prior research.

claim: Expression of all nine fz receptors was observed within piwi-1+ ASCs in between the two brain lobes.
source: These in silico findings were also confirmed by performing dFISH experiments, which showed expression of all nine fz receptors within piwi-1+ ASCs in between the two brain lobes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on dFISH experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Planarian stem cells adjacent to the CNS are one of the cellular targets of brain-derived hh and Wnt signals.
source: Taken together, these dFISH and in silico data suggested that planarian stem cells adjacent to the CNS are one of the cellular targets of brain-derived hh and Wnt signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dFISH and single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Planarian transcription factors are expressed not only by the cells and tissues that they act to specify, but also within ASCs nearby the mature organ in question.
source: Recent studies have highlighted an interesting property of planarian transcription factors: they are expressed not only by the cells and tissues that they act to specify, but also within ASCs nearby the mature organ in question (Currie and Pearson, 2013; Cowles et al., 2013; Scimone et al., 2011, 2014; Lapan and Reddien, 2011, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Expression of nkx2.1 or arx was observed within a significant number of stem cells or post-mitotic progenitors in the region between the brain lobes.
source: In this specific spatial region, expression of nkx2.1 or arx was observed within a significant number of stem cells or post-mitotic progenitors (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: This is based on dFISH combined with immunolabeling experiments shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: 7.99 ± 0.95% of piwi-1+ stem cells displayed expression of nkx2.1.
source: Quantification of piwi-1+ stem cells revealed that a significant percentage displayed expression of nkx2.1 (7.99 ± 0.95%), whereas arx expression was less frequent (1.74 ± 0.99%).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH combined with immunolabeling experiments.

claim: 1.74 ± 0.99% of piwi-1+ stem cells displayed expression of arx.
source: Quantification of piwi-1+ stem cells revealed that a significant percentage displayed expression of nkx2.1 (7.99 ± 0.95%), whereas arx expression was less frequent (1.74 ± 0.99%).
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH combined with immunolabeling experiments.

claim: 13.29 ± 1.96% of all PIWI-1+ cells (encompassing both stem cells and their post-mitotic progeny) expressed nkx2.1.
source: Quantification of all PIWI-1+ cells (encompassing both stem cells and their post-mitotic progeny) demonstrated an expansion of nkx2.1 and arx expression, to include 13.29 ± 1.96% and 8.11 ± 1.83%, respectively, of all cells counted.
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH combined with immunolabeling experiments.

claim: 8.11 ± 1.83% of all PIWI-1+ cells (encompassing both stem cells and their post-mitotic progeny) expressed arx.
source: Quantification of all PIWI-1+ cells (encompassing both stem cells and their post-mitotic progeny) demonstrated an expansion of nkx2.1 and arx expression, to include 13.29 ± 1.96% and 8.11 ± 1.83%, respectively, of all cells counted.
evidence: This is quantitative data from dFISH combined with immunolabeling experiments.

claim: 31 out of 168 sequenced head stem cells (X1 and X2) expressed at least one of nkx2.1 or arx.
source: Both nkx2.1 and arx were found to be expressed within these cells and a total of 31/168 cells expressed at least one factor (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells demonstrated high expression levels of established stem cell markers/regulators and cell cycle genes.
source: Importantly, nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells demonstrated high expression levels of established stem cell markers/regulators (piwi-1, piwi-2, piwi-3, Smed-bruli, Smed-tdrd1L2, Smed-chd4), and cell cycle genes (Smed-mcm2, Smed-pcna, Smed-cyclinB-2) (Figure 5G) (Zhu et al., 2015; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2006; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5G, with citations to prior research.

claim: Many nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells displayed expression of established and putative neuronal transcription factors and mature neural markers.
source: In addition, many cells displayed expression of established and putative neuronal transcription factors (Smed-coe, Smed-cas, Smed-hb-2, Smed-mitfl-2, Smed-da, Smed-isl-1) and mature neural markers (Smed-synapsin, Smed-pc-2) (Figure 5G) (Cowles et al., 2013, 2014; Hayashi et al., 2011; Scimone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5G, with citations to prior research.

claim: 7 out of 31 nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells exhibited expression of ptc, smo, or gli-1.
source: Several of these nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells also exhibited expression of ptc, smo, or gli-1 (7/31 cells) and at least one of the nine fz receptors (14/31) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 14 out of 31 nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells exhibited expression of at least one of the nine fz receptors.
source: Several of these nkx2.1+ or arx+ stem cells also exhibited expression of ptc, smo, or gli-1 (7/31 cells) and at least one of the nine fz receptors (14/31) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ptc expression within nkx2.1+ and arx+ neural progenitors was observed in vivo based on dFISH combined with immunostaining against the PIWI-1 protein.
source: Finally, ptc expression within nkx2.1+ and arx+ neural progenitors was also observed in vivo based on dFISH combined with immunostaining against the PIWI-1 protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on dFISH combined with immunolabeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Putative neural progenitor cells, located adjacent to the mature brain, express the machinery to transduce hh signals and may be committed to producing arx+ or nkx2.1+ neurons.
source: Together, these data demonstrated that putative neural progenitor cells, located adjacent to the mature brain, express the machinery to transduce hh signals and may be committed to producing arx+ or nkx2.1+ neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dFISH and single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Silencing of the planarian hh ligand resulted in a significant reduction of expression for all five neural transcription factors (nkx2.1, arx, lhx1/5–1, coe, and pax6a) within PIWI-1+ cells.
source: Silencing of the planarian hh ligand resulted in a significant reduction of expression for all five neural transcription factors within PIWI-1+ cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Levels of neural progenitor cells were largely unchanged in ptc(RNAi) animals, with the exception of coe and pax6a which exhibited a small but significant increase in PIWI-1+ cells.
source: In contrast, levels of neural progenitor cells were largely unchanged in ptc(RNAi) animals, with the exception of coe and pax6a which exhibited a small but significant increase in PIWI-1+ cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is quantitative data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: hh(RNAi) animals consistently displayed significantly lower cholinergic neural homeostasis both after 6-day (~35% reduction) and 9-day chase periods (>40% reduction).
source: hh(RNAi) animals consistently displayed significantly lower cholinergic neural homeostasis both after 6-day (~35% reduction) and 9-day chase periods (>40% reduction), while silencing of ptc had little effect (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from BrdU pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Silencing of ptc had little effect on cholinergic neural homeostasis.
source: hh(RNAi) animals consistently displayed significantly lower cholinergic neural homeostasis both after 6-day (~35% reduction) and 9-day chase periods (>40% reduction), while silencing of ptc had little effect (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is quantitative data from BrdU pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Decreased hh signaling did not affect the intact population of any neuronal cell type after long-term RNAi (10 feedings).
source: To investigate whether this decrease in neuronal homeostasis levels affected the intact nervous system, long-term RNAi experiments were performed (10 feedings), and all five neuronal populations were examined. Of particular interest were the VM cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neural populations, which express the hh ligand (Figure 3C–E). However, decreased hh signaling did not affect the intact population of any neuronal cell type (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2; see Discussion).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Planarian tissues (eyes, pharynx, epidermis, and gut) were largely unaffected by perturbations to hh signaling, except for the eyes, which exhibited reduced progenitor cell numbers in hh(RNAi) animals, and increased BrdU incorporation after ptc knockdown.
source: To determine whether brain-derived hh signals were required specifically to maintain normal levels of neurogenesis, or whether this ligand acts globally to stimulate the production of all planarian cell types, progenitor cells and BrdU incorporation were examined for four additional tissues; the eyes, pharynx, epidermis, and gut. Importantly, these other planarian tissues were largely unaffected by perturbations to hh signaling, except for the eyes, which exhibited reduced progenitor cell numbers in hh(RNAi) animals, and increased BrdU incorporation after ptc knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Neuronal sources of the planarian hh ligand specifically regulate their own homeostasis through distinct progenitors in the uninjured brain.
source: These combined experiments, demonstrated that neuronal sources of the planarian hh ligand specifically regulate their own homeostasis through distinct progenitors in the uninjured brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi and BrdU experiments showing specific effects on neurogenesis.

claim: nkx2.1 and arx function in the long-term maintenance of cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons in the VM region of the planarian CNS.
source: This work has demonstrated that two planarian homeodomain transcription factor homologs, nkx2.1 and arx, function in the long-term maintenance of cholinergic, GABAergic, and octopaminergic neurons in the VM region of the planarian CNS (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: All four of the sequenced hh+ neurons co-expressed a planarian Wnt ligand, Smed-wnt11-6.
source: Neuronal hh expression was also confirmed by using a scRNAseq dataset that included mature neurons (Wurtzel et al., 2015), and additionally revealed that all four of the sequenced hh+ neurons co-expressed a planarian Wnt ligand, Smed-wnt11-6 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3I, with a citation to prior research.

claim: Similar to planarian muscle cells, many mature planarian neurons express hh and Wnt ligands which regulate neurogenesis levels and maintain patterning.
source: Similar to planarian muscle cells, many of which express important signaling molecules that maintain positional control along the body axis and during regeneration events (Witchley et al., 2013; Scimone et al., 2016), mature planarian neurons express hh and Wnt ligands which regulate neurogenesis levels and maintain patterning (Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the findings and citations to prior research.

claim: The Wnt ligand Smed-wnt11-6 and Wnt antagonist Smed-notum are expressed by cholinergic neurons.
source: Previous studies have shown that the Wnt ligand Smed-wnt11-6 and Wnt antagonist Smed-notum are expressed by cholinergic neurons, and that this Wnt signal acts on planarian stem cells to repress neuron production and prevent posterior expansion of brain tissue during regeneration (Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The Wnt signal from cholinergic neurons acts on planarian stem cells to repress neuron production and prevent posterior expansion of brain tissue during regeneration.
source: Previous studies have shown that the Wnt ligand Smed-wnt11-6 and Wnt antagonist Smed-notum are expressed by cholinergic neurons, and that this Wnt signal acts on planarian stem cells to repress neuron production and prevent posterior expansion of brain tissue during regeneration (Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Several planarian neurons simultaneously express the repressive Wnt ligand Smed-wnt11-6 as well as the hh signaling molecule, which promotes the production of neurons.
source: Interestingly, we show that several planarian neurons simultaneously express this repressive Wnt ligand as well as the hh signaling molecule, which promotes the production of neurons (Figures 3I and 6G).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data and the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neuronal sources of hh actively promote neurogenesis levels in both the brain and of eye photoreceptors neurons.
source: However, our observations suggest that contrary to this model, neuronal sources of hh actively promote neurogenesis levels in both the brain and of eye photoreceptors neurons (Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Long-term hh(RNAi) did not produce robust neural deficits over a span of five weeks.
source: Similar to mechanisms of Hh action in other systems, the regulatory loops are likely to be complex in planarians due to the fact that long-term hh(RNAi), surprisingly, did not produce robust neural deficits over a span of five weeks (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: With body-wide changes in proliferation in hh(RNAi), rates of neural cell death may also be decreased, leading to little change in neuronal populations.
source: Perhaps with body-wide changes in proliferation in hh(RNAi), rates of neural cell death are also decreased, leading to little change in neuronal populations (Rink et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results, with a citation to prior research.

claim: In the mammalian CNS, expression of Shh from differentiating and mature neurons is required to maintain normal proliferation levels of embryonic neural precursors and adult neural stem cells, respectively.
source: Similarly, in the mammalian CNS, expression of Shh from differentiating and mature neurons is required to maintain normal proliferation levels of embryonic neural precursors and adult neural stem cells, respectively (Álvarez-Buylla and Ihrie, 2014; Ihrie et al., 2011; Fuccillo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Planarian neural-biased stem cells are situated in the mesenchymal space in between the two brain lobes.
source: Unlike most organisms where neural stem cells are packed within an organized neuroepithelium, planarian neural-biased stem cells are situated in the mesenchymal space in between the two brain lobes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neural-committed stem cells, termed νNeoblasts, were recently detected computationally.
source: Computationally, neural-committed stem cells, termed νNeoblasts, were recently detected and may be the targets of brain-derived signals (Molinaro and Pearson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In chordate nerve cord development, Hh is expressed ventrally, along the long body axis and has strong ventralizing roles in cell fate determination.
source: In chordate nerve cord development, Hh is expressed ventrally, along the long body axis and has strong ventralizing roles in cell fate determination (Briscoe and Ericson, 2001; Jessell, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ventral Hh expression and ventralizing roles in cell fate determination is not typical of arthropods.
source: This is not typical of arthropods (Matise, 2007; Arendt and Nübler-Jung, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VM neural fates in planarians may be specified using mechanisms more associated with chordates.
source: It is interesting to speculate that VM neural fates in planarians are specified using mechanisms more associated with chordates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings.

claim: In the embryonic rodent ventral telencephalon, Nkx2.1 acts in upstream neural progenitor cells to produce both cortical GABAergic interneurons and striatal cholinergic interneurons.
source: In the embryonic rodent ventral telencephalon, Nkx2.1 acts in upstream neural progenitor cells to produce both cortical GABAergic interneurons and striatal cholinergic interneurons (Butt et al., 2008; Lopes et al., 2012; Sussel et al., 1999), whereas Arx functions downstream in the terminal differentiation and migration of cortical GABAergic interneurons (Vogt et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the embryonic rodent ventral telencephalon, Arx functions downstream in the terminal differentiation and migration of cortical GABAergic interneurons.
source: In the embryonic rodent ventral telencephalon, Nkx2.1 acts in upstream neural progenitor cells to produce both cortical GABAergic interneurons and striatal cholinergic interneurons (Butt et al., 2008; Lopes et al., 2012; Sussel et al., 1999), whereas Arx functions downstream in the terminal differentiation and migration of cortical GABAergic interneurons (Vogt et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The planarian transcription factors nkx2.1 and arx have retained a remarkable degree of functional conservation with their mammalian counterparts across a significant evolutionary gap.
source: Notwithstanding this slight deviation in cell fate determinism, it appears that these two transcription factors have retained a remarkable degree of functional conservation across this significant evolutionary gap.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of planarian and mammalian transcription factor functions.
